Key clarifying finding: cargo-dist's npm installer is a single wrapper package that fetches from GitHub Releases at install time via postinstall — it is *not* the esbuild/Claude-Code-style optionalDependencies-per-platform pattern. For the "true" optionalDependencies pattern with Rust binaries, `cargo-npm` is the dedicated tool. This is the most important nuance to flag.

# Shipping `deadreckon`: packaging, distribution, self-update

Researched May 2026. Goal: lowest-friction install across macOS/Linux (and Windows nice-to-have) + a self-update story. Special focus on the "ship a Rust binary through bun/npm" question.

## 1. The npm/bun pattern (how Claude Code, esbuild, swc, biome, turbo, rolldown do it)

The pattern is **one wrapper package + N platform-specific packages declared as `optionalDependencies`** with `os`/`cpu` filters. Each platform package contains a single prebuilt native binary. npm/bun/pnpm resolves only the matching one for the current host; a tiny postinstall shim (or `bin` entry resolving to the right path) execs the binary.

Claude Code switched to this in v2.1.113 (Nov 2025): `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code` pulls e.g. `@anthropic-ai/claude-code-darwin-arm64` via optional dependency, postinstall links it. Supported targets include `darwin-arm64/x64`, `linux-x64/arm64` (+ musl variants), `win32-x64/arm64`. ([npm page](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@anthropic-ai/claude-code), [Chainthink writeup](https://chainthink.cn/en/article/124567507032707072))

esbuild's `optionalDependencies` PR (#1621) is the canonical reference for *why* this beats a postinstall-download approach: works with custom registries, offline caches, read-only FS, and `--ignore-scripts`. ([esbuild PR #1621](https://github.com/evanw/esbuild/pull/1621), [deepwiki summary](https://deepwiki.com/evanw/esbuild/6.2-platform-specific-binaries))

**Minimal shape — wrapper `package.json`:**

```json
{
  "name": "deadreckon",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "bin": { "deadreckon": "bin/deadreckon.js" },
  "optionalDependencies": {
    "deadreckon-darwin-arm64": "0.1.0",
    "deadreckon-darwin-x64":   "0.1.0",
    "deadreckon-linux-x64":    "0.1.0",
    "deadreckon-linux-arm64":  "0.1.0",
    "deadreckon-win32-x64":    "0.1.0"
  }
}
```

**Platform package `package.json`:**

```json
{
  "name": "deadreckon-darwin-arm64",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "os": ["darwin"],
  "cpu": ["arm64"],
  "bin": { "deadreckon": "bin/deadreckon" }
}
```

The wrapper's `bin/deadreckon.js` just `require.resolve`s the platform package and `execFileSync`s its binary (or a postinstall renames it into place, esbuild-style).

**Is bun special?** No — bun is npm-registry-compatible and honors `optionalDependencies` + `os`/`cpu`. Bun 1.2 added `--cpu` / `--os` flags to *force* a target (useful for Docker cross-installs), and stores normalized cpu/os in `bun.lock` so the lockfile is portable while the installed set differs per host. ([bun install docs](https://bun.com/docs/pm/cli/install), [Bun v1.2.23 blog](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.2.23)) End-user UX is just `bun install -g deadreckon` or `bunx deadreckon`. No bun-specific bundling step (`bun build --compile`) is needed — that's for compiling JS, not for shipping a Rust binary.

Gotcha: if a user installs with `--ignore-scripts` *and* `--omit=optional` you're hosed. The Claude Code issue tracker has live examples ([anthropics/claude-code#50974](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/50974)).

## 2. Tooling that automates this for Rust

| Tool | What it does | Fit for deadreckon |
|---|---|---|
| **`cargo-dist` / `dist`** (axodotdev) | One-command release pipeline: GitHub Actions matrix, archives, shell+powershell installers, Homebrew tap, MSI, npm installer, axoupdater. v0.31.0 (Feb 2026). ([repo](https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist), [JS quickstart](https://axodotdev.github.io/cargo-dist/book/quickstart/javascript.html)) | **Primary recommendation.** But its `npm` installer is a *single wrapper that downloads from GitHub Releases via postinstall* — not the optionalDependencies-per-platform pattern. ([npm installer docs](https://axodotdev.github.io/cargo-dist/book/installers/npm.html)) |
| **`cargo-npm`** | Generates the exact esbuild/Claude-Code pattern: wrapper + N platform packages with optionalDependencies, *no* postinstall download. ([repo](https://github.com/abemedia/cargo-npm)) | Use this if you want the Claude-Code-grade npm UX (works behind `--ignore-scripts`, offline caches, corporate proxies). |
| **`cross`** | Docker-based cross-compile for Linux targets. | Use inside CI for `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` etc. |
| **`cargo-zigbuild`** | Uses zig as the linker; great for glibc-version-pinned Linux builds and macOS universal2. | Often *the* fix for "binary requires glibc 2.34" complaints. dist supports it. |
| **`cargo-binstall`** | End-user installer: `cargo binstall deadreckon` fetches your GitHub release. ([repo](https://github.com/cargo-bins/cargo-binstall)) | Free if you publish to crates.io + GitHub Releases with predictable names. dist emits compatible metadata. |
| **`napi-rs`** | Native Node *addons*. | **Not applicable** — that's for `.node` modules, not standalone CLIs. |
| **`tauri` bundler** | App bundles for GUI apps. | **Not applicable** for a TUI. |

**The "one command, all platforms + npm wrapper" answer is `dist`.** Caveat: if you specifically want the optionalDependencies pattern (recommended — matches what Claude Code ships), layer `cargo-npm` on top, or post-process the dist artifacts into platform packages yourself in CI. There's an open dist issue to adopt the optionalDependencies pattern but it hasn't shipped.

**Concrete commands with `dist`:**

```bash
cargo install cargo-dist          # or: curl -LsSf https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/releases/latest/download/cargo-dist-installer.sh | sh
dist init                          # interactive; pick shell, powershell, homebrew, npm, msi; enable updater
dist plan                          # dry-run: shows the matrix
dist build                         # builds locally for the current host
git tag v0.1.0 && git push --tags  # CI (generated workflow) does the real release
```

`dist init` writes a `[workspace.metadata.dist]` block; the generated GitHub Actions workflow fans out across `aarch64-apple-darwin`, `x86_64-apple-darwin`, `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu`, `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`, publishes archives + checksums + installers to the GitHub Release, and (if enabled) pushes an npm package and a Homebrew tap.

## 3. Self-update

- **`axoupdater`** (built into dist): set `install-updater = true` and dist ships a sibling binary `deadreckon-update`, or you embed axoupdater as a crate and add a `deadreckon update` subcommand. It checks GitHub Releases and re-runs the installer. ([axoupdater repo](https://github.com/axodotdev/axoupdater), [updater docs](https://axodotdev.github.io/cargo-dist/book/installers/updater.html))
- **`self_update` crate** (jaemk, v0.42+, rustls feature available): manual approach — query GitHub Releases API, download archive, swap binary. ([repo](https://github.com/jaemk/self_update))
- **Package-manager updates**: `bun update -g deadreckon`, `brew upgrade deadreckon`, `cargo binstall --force deadreckon`. Free, but only works for users who installed that way.
- **What Claude Code does**: ships a built-in `claude update` (auto-prompts on stale versions). Mechanism differs by install channel — npm users get an npm-channel update; native-installer users get a binary-swap update. The cross-platform bugs are real ([#50962](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/50962)).

Trade-off: axoupdater/self_update give you a one-command UX you control (`deadreckon update`) but inherit macOS Gatekeeper pain on the swapped binary. Package-manager updates dodge that but require the user to remember which channel they used.

## 4. macOS signing/notarization — the unavoidable tax

Unsigned binaries downloaded outside the App Store get the `com.apple.quarantine` xattr and Gatekeeper blocks them with "cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified." For a CLI/TUI you need:

1. Apple Developer Program membership ($99/yr) → Developer ID Application certificate.
2. `codesign --sign "Developer ID Application: …" --options runtime --timestamp deadreckon`.
3. Zip and submit: `xcrun notarytool submit deadreckon.zip --apple-id … --team-id … --password … --wait`.
4. Staple to the archive if it's a `.pkg`/`.dmg` (CLI binaries can't be stapled directly; the archive can).

dist has an open codesign issue ([#1121](https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/issues/1121)) — you'll likely run codesign/notarytool yourself in the GitHub Actions workflow dist generates. Users installing via Homebrew or via `bun install` (the binary lives under `node_modules` rather than being a direct download) often skip the quarantine flag because the package manager wrote the file, not Safari — but don't rely on that; sign it.

## 5. Recommendation for `deadreckon`

Your prior is correct, with one adjustment. Use:

1. **`dist` for the build/release pipeline** — `dist init`, tag, push, done. Enable installers `["shell", "powershell", "homebrew", "npm"]` and `install-updater = true`. This gives you:
   - `curl -LsSf https://github.com/you/deadreckon/releases/latest/download/deadreckon-installer.sh | sh` (macOS+Linux)
   - `brew install you/tap/deadreckon`
   - `cargo binstall deadreckon` (free)
2. **For the npm/bun channel, decide:**
   - *Quick path*: ship dist's built-in npm installer. UX is `bun install -g deadreckon` → wrapper postinstalls a binary from GitHub Releases. Works for 95% of users.
   - *Claude-Code-grade path*: also publish via `cargo-npm` (or a small CI script that splits dist's archives into platform packages) so you get the optionalDependencies pattern. This is what survives `--ignore-scripts`, corporate proxies, and matches what Anthropic ships.
3. **Self-update**: embed `axoupdater` as a crate and wire `deadreckon update` as a clap subcommand. End user runs `deadreckon update`. For users on the npm/bun channel, document `bun update -g deadreckon` as the alternative — and have `deadreckon update` detect the install source and print the right hint rather than swapping a binary it doesn't own.
4. **macOS**: codesign + notarize in the dist-generated GitHub Actions workflow. Budget half a day to set up `APPLE_ID`, `TEAM_ID`, app-specific password, and the Developer ID cert as repo secrets.
5. **Linux glibc**: build with `cargo-zigbuild` (dist supports it) targeting glibc 2.17/2.28 so you don't get bug reports from Debian stable users.

End-user UX, by channel:

```
# macOS / Linux one-liner
curl -LsSf https://github.com/you/deadreckon/releases/latest/download/deadreckon-installer.sh | sh

# bun / npm / pnpm
bun install -g deadreckon
npx deadreckon          # or: bunx deadreckon

# Homebrew
brew install you/tap/deadreckon

# Rust users
cargo binstall deadreckon

# Update (any channel)
deadreckon update
```

Based on the search results, here's how Claude Code's npm distribution with optionalDependencies and platform-specific binaries works:

## How It Works

npm pulls the binary in through a per-platform optional dependency such as @anthropic-ai/claude-code-darwin-arm64, and a postinstall step links it into place. 

Starting from version v2.1.113, Claude Code's npm distribution package has been replaced from JavaScript build artifacts to native binaries for each platform. The installation command npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code remains unchanged; npm will automatically fetch the corresponding pre-compiled binary based on the platform via optional dependency and complete the linking through a postinstall script.

## Supported Platforms

Supported npm install platforms are darwin-arm64, darwin-x64, linux-x64, linux-arm64, linux-x64-musl, linux-arm64-musl, win32-x64, and win32-arm64.

## Key Requirements

Your package manager must allow optional dependencies. If installation fails, the error message indicates that either postinstall did not run (--ignore-scripts, some pnpm configs) or the platform-native optional dependency was not downloaded (--omit=optional).

## Benefits

This change brings two direct optimizations: first, improved startup speed by eliminating cold start overhead associated with Node.js parsing and compilation; second, runtime no longer depends on a locally installed Node.js, thus avoiding issues caused by Node.js version discrepancies, significantly reducing installation failures and environment conflicts.

Based on the search results, here's comprehensive information about esbuild's npm optionalDependencies pattern for platform-specific binaries:

## Overview

esbuild uses an install script and depends on a separate optional package for each platform-specific binary executable. The installation strategy automatically downloads the correct binary executable using npm's optionalDependencies feature to depend on all esbuild packages for all platforms but only have the one for the current platform be installed.

## The Pattern

esbuild provides native binaries for a comprehensive set of platform combinations, distributed as scoped npm packages under @esbuild/, where each package contains a single pre-compiled binary for its target platform. The main esbuild package declares all platform packages as optionalDependencies, allowing npm to gracefully handle installation failures for unsupported platforms.

## Why This Approach?

This installation strategy improves compatibility with edge cases such as custom registries, custom proxies, offline installations, read-only file systems, or when post-install scripts are disabled, replacing the old installation strategy which manually downloaded the correct binary executable in a post-install script.

## Installation Behavior

The esbuild binary for the current platform is automatically selected and installed from esbuild's optional dependencies by npm. There is still a small post-install script that is optional, which optimizes the installed package by replacing the esbuild JavaScript command shim with the actual binary executable at install time.

## Important Flags to Avoid

When installing esbuild with npm, make sure you don't specify the "--no-optional" or "--omit=optional" flags, as the optionalDependencies feature is used to install the correct binary executable for your current platform.

For JavaScript CLI applications, cargo-dist currently:

- **`dist init --yes`**: Generates configuration interactively, creates CI workflows
- **`dist build`**: Builds for your current platform, outputs archives and installer scripts
- **`dist plan`**: Shows what all platforms will build without actually compiling

[workspace]

```

# cargo-dist Self-Update Story

cargo-dist itself doesn't have a `dist selfupdate` command. Instead, the tool provides a mechanism for **your distributed software** to self-update.

## How It Works

When you add `install-updater = true` to your `Cargo.toml`, dist includes a standalone updater program with shell and PowerShell installers. This updater is built on the open-source [axoupdater](https://github.com/axodotdev/axoupdater) project.

## What End Users Run

End users invoke the updater by running:
```
yourpackage-update
```

Or, if your program supports custom subcommands (like git or cargo):
```
yourpackage update
```

The updater requires no options or arguments and automatically checks for new releases and installs them without further user interaction.

## For Library Use

If you want to handle update polling yourself within your application, axoupdater is also available as a [Rust crate](https://crates.io/crates/axoupdater) that can be integrated directly into your program's codebase.

The search results provide comprehensive information about how Bun handles `optionalDependencies` with platform and binary compatibility. Here's what I found:

## Platform-Specific Optional Dependencies

Bun stores normalized CPU and OS values from npm in the lockfile and skips downloading, extracting, and installing packages disabled for the current target at runtime. The lockfile won't change between platforms/architectures even if the packages ultimately installed do change.

## Control Over Platform-Specific Dependencies

You can now control which platform-specific optionalDependencies are installed using the new `--cpu` and `--os` flags in bun install. This is useful when you're installing dependencies for a different target environment, such as in a Docker container or CI/CD pipeline, and you can provide multiple values to install dependencies for several targets at once.

For example: "Install optional dependencies for a Linux ARM64 target: `bun install --os linux --cpu arm64`"

## Configuration via bunfig.toml

Bun installs all dependencies, devDependencies, and optionalDependencies by default. You can configure this in bunfig.toml with `[install]` section where `optional = true` controls whether to install optionalDependencies.

## General Compatibility

Accepted values for `--cpu` are: arm64, x64, ia32, ppc64, s390x; and for `--os`: linux, darwin, win32, freebsd, openbsd, sunos, aix.

# cargo-dist npm Installer

## Overview

The npm installer in cargo-dist automatically generates and publishes npm packages for Rust binaries. Users can then install applications globally via `npm install -g @scope/package` or run them immediately with `npx @scope/package`.

## How It Works

The generated npm package acts as a wrapper that "fetches your prebuilt archives and install your binaries to node_modules, exposing them as commands." If the package contains a single unambiguous binary, it can be executed directly via `npx` without specifying the command name.

## Configuration

To enable npm publishing, users run `dist init` and select "npm" as an installer option. The resulting workspace configuration looks like:

```toml
[workspace.metadata.dist]
installers = ["npm"]
npm-scope = "@axodotdev"
publish-jobs = ["npm"]
```

Optional package metadata improves the npm listing:

```toml
[package]
description = "a CLI for learning to distribute CLIs in rust"
homepage = "https://github.com/axodotdev/axolotlsay"
```

## Advanced Options

**Custom Package Names**: The `npm-package` setting allows renaming the published package independently of the Cargo package name.

**Dependency Locking**: By default, dependencies lock via `npm-shrinkwrap.json` for reproducible installations. This can be disabled with `npm-shrinkwrap = false` to allow newer dependency versions.

## User Experience

After setup, users see installation hints like:

```
npm install @axodotdev/cargodisttest@0.2.0
```

## Key Findings

**cargo-npm** appears to be the most relevant tool matching your query. Users install the main package via npm - it pulls in only the binary for their platform as an optional dependency and runs it transparently.

### How cargo-npm Works

cargo-npm generates individual npm packages for each target platform (e.g., my-tool-linux-x64), with each package containing the pre-compiled binary for that specific platform, eliminating the need for runtime downloads. 

A main package acts as the entry point, listing the platform-specific packages as optionalDependencies, and during installation, npm's native dependency resolution mechanism automatically selects and downloads the package matching the host system's architecture.

### Comparison with cargo-dist

While traditional approaches to Rust CLI distribution via npm often involve tools like cargo-dist, which typically rely on postinstall scripts embedded within the npm package that download pre-compiled binaries from external sources like GitHub Releases, cargo-npm takes a different approach that avoids postinstall scripts entirely.

### Related Information

The optionalDependencies field is for dependencies that can be used but not strictly needed for the package, with target-specific NPM packages specified in this field to ensure only the appropriate package for the current architecture is installed.

# Shipping `deadreckon`: packaging, distribution, self-update

Researched May 2026. Goal: lowest-friction install across macOS/Linux (and Windows nice-to-have) + a self-update story. Special focus on the "ship a Rust binary through bun/npm" question.

## 1. The npm/bun pattern (how Claude Code, esbuild, swc, biome, turbo, rolldown do it)

The pattern is **one wrapper package + N platform-specific packages declared as `optionalDependencies`** with `os`/`cpu` filters. Each platform package contains a single prebuilt native binary. npm/bun/pnpm resolves only the matching one for the current host; a tiny postinstall shim (or `bin` entry resolving to the right path) execs the binary.

Claude Code switched to this in v2.1.113 (Nov 2025): `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code` pulls e.g. `@anthropic-ai/claude-code-darwin-arm64` via optional dependency, postinstall links it. Supported targets include `darwin-arm64/x64`, `linux-x64/arm64` (+ musl variants), `win32-x64/arm64`. ([npm page](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@anthropic-ai/claude-code), [Chainthink writeup](https://chainthink.cn/en/article/124567507032707072))

esbuild's `optionalDependencies` PR (#1621) is the canonical reference for *why* this beats a postinstall-download approach: works with custom registries, offline caches, read-only FS, and `--ignore-scripts`. ([esbuild PR #1621](https://github.com/evanw/esbuild/pull/1621), [deepwiki summary](https://deepwiki.com/evanw/esbuild/6.2-platform-specific-binaries))

**Minimal shape — wrapper `package.json`:**

```json
{
  "name": "deadreckon",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "bin": { "deadreckon": "bin/deadreckon.js" },
  "optionalDependencies": {
    "deadreckon-darwin-arm64": "0.1.0",
    "deadreckon-darwin-x64":   "0.1.0",
    "deadreckon-linux-x64":    "0.1.0",
    "deadreckon-linux-arm64":  "0.1.0",
    "deadreckon-win32-x64":    "0.1.0"
  }
}
```

**Platform package `package.json`:**

```json
{
  "name": "deadreckon-darwin-arm64",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "os": ["darwin"],
  "cpu": ["arm64"],
  "bin": { "deadreckon": "bin/deadreckon" }
}
```

The wrapper's `bin/deadreckon.js` just `require.resolve`s the platform package and `execFileSync`s its binary (or a postinstall renames it into place, esbuild-style).

**Is bun special?** No — bun is npm-registry-compatible and honors `optionalDependencies` + `os`/`cpu`. Bun 1.2 added `--cpu` / `--os` flags to *force* a target (useful for Docker cross-installs), and stores normalized cpu/os in `bun.lock` so the lockfile is portable while the installed set differs per host. ([bun install docs](https://bun.com/docs/pm/cli/install), [Bun v1.2.23 blog](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.2.23)) End-user UX is just `bun install -g deadreckon` or `bunx deadreckon`. No bun-specific bundling step (`bun build --compile`) is needed — that's for compiling JS, not for shipping a Rust binary.

Gotcha: if a user installs with `--ignore-scripts` *and* `--omit=optional` you're hosed. The Claude Code issue tracker has live examples ([anthropics/claude-code#50974](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/50974)).

## 2. Tooling that automates this for Rust

| Tool | What it does | Fit for deadreckon |
|---|---|---|
| **`cargo-dist` / `dist`** (axodotdev) | One-command release pipeline: GitHub Actions matrix, archives, shell+powershell installers, Homebrew tap, MSI, npm installer, axoupdater. v0.31.0 (Feb 2026). ([repo](https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist), [JS quickstart](https://axodotdev.github.io/cargo-dist/book/quickstart/javascript.html)) | **Primary recommendation.** But its `npm` installer is a *single wrapper that downloads from GitHub Releases via postinstall* — not the optionalDependencies-per-platform pattern. ([npm installer docs](https://axodotdev.github.io/cargo-dist/book/installers/npm.html)) |
| **`cargo-npm`** | Generates the exact esbuild/Claude-Code pattern: wrapper + N platform packages with optionalDependencies, *no* postinstall download. ([repo](https://github.com/abemedia/cargo-npm)) | Use this if you want the Claude-Code-grade npm UX (works behind `--ignore-scripts`, offline caches, corporate proxies). |
| **`cross`** | Docker-based cross-compile for Linux targets. | Use inside CI for `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` etc. |
| **`cargo-zigbuild`** | Uses zig as the linker; great for glibc-version-pinned Linux builds and macOS universal2. | Often *the* fix for "binary requires glibc 2.34" complaints. dist supports it. |
| **`cargo-binstall`** | End-user installer: `cargo binstall deadreckon` fetches your GitHub release. ([repo](https://github.com/cargo-bins/cargo-binstall)) | Free if you publish to crates.io + GitHub Releases with predictable names. dist emits compatible metadata. |
| **`napi-rs`** | Native Node *addons*. | **Not applicable** — that's for `.node` modules, not standalone CLIs. |
| **`tauri` bundler** | App bundles for GUI apps. | **Not applicable** for a TUI. |

**The "one command, all platforms + npm wrapper" answer is `dist`.** Caveat: if you specifically want the optionalDependencies pattern (recommended — matches what Claude Code ships), layer `cargo-npm` on top, or post-process the dist artifacts into platform packages yourself in CI. There's an open dist issue to adopt the optionalDependencies pattern but it hasn't shipped.

**Concrete commands with `dist`:**

```bash
cargo install cargo-dist          # or: curl -LsSf https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/releases/latest/download/cargo-dist-installer.sh | sh
dist init                          # interactive; pick shell, powershell, homebrew, npm, msi; enable updater
dist plan                          # dry-run: shows the matrix
dist build                         # builds locally for the current host
git tag v0.1.0 && git push --tags  # CI (generated workflow) does the real release
```

`dist init` writes a `[workspace.metadata.dist]` block; the generated GitHub Actions workflow fans out across `aarch64-apple-darwin`, `x86_64-apple-darwin`, `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu`, `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`, publishes archives + checksums + installers to the GitHub Release, and (if enabled) pushes an npm package and a Homebrew tap.

## 3. Self-update

- **`axoupdater`** (built into dist): set `install-updater = true` and dist ships a sibling binary `deadreckon-update`, or you embed axoupdater as a crate and add a `deadreckon update` subcommand. It checks GitHub Releases and re-runs the installer. ([axoupdater repo](https://github.com/axodotdev/axoupdater), [updater docs](https://axodotdev.github.io/cargo-dist/book/installers/updater.html))
- **`self_update` crate** (jaemk, v0.42+, rustls feature available): manual approach — query GitHub Releases API, download archive, swap binary. ([repo](https://github.com/jaemk/self_update))
- **Package-manager updates**: `bun update -g deadreckon`, `brew upgrade deadreckon`, `cargo binstall --force deadreckon`. Free, but only works for users who installed that way.
- **What Claude Code does**: ships a built-in `claude update` (auto-prompts on stale versions). Mechanism differs by install channel — npm users get an npm-channel update; native-installer users get a binary-swap update. The cross-platform bugs are real ([#50962](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/50962)).

Trade-off: axoupdater/self_update give you a one-command UX you control (`deadreckon update`) but inherit macOS Gatekeeper pain on the swapped binary. Package-manager updates dodge that but require the user to remember which channel they used.

## 4. macOS signing/notarization — the unavoidable tax

Unsigned binaries downloaded outside the App Store get the `com.apple.quarantine` xattr and Gatekeeper blocks them with "cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified." For a CLI/TUI you need:

1. Apple Developer Program membership ($99/yr) → Developer ID Application certificate.
2. `codesign --sign "Developer ID Application: …" --options runtime --timestamp deadreckon`.
3. Zip and submit: `xcrun notarytool submit deadreckon.zip --apple-id … --team-id … --password … --wait`.
4. Staple to the archive if it's a `.pkg`/`.dmg` (CLI binaries can't be stapled directly; the archive can).

dist has an open codesign issue ([#1121](https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist/issues/1121)) — you'll likely run codesign/notarytool yourself in the GitHub Actions workflow dist generates. Users installing via Homebrew or via `bun install` (the binary lives under `node_modules` rather than being a direct download) often skip the quarantine flag because the package manager wrote the file, not Safari — but don't rely on that; sign it.

## 5. Recommendation for `deadreckon`

Your prior is correct, with one adjustment. Use:

1. **`dist` for the build/release pipeline** — `dist init`, tag, push, done. Enable installers `["shell", "powershell", "homebrew", "npm"]` and `install-updater = true`. This gives you:
   - `curl -LsSf https://github.com/you/deadreckon/releases/latest/download/deadreckon-installer.sh | sh` (macOS+Linux)
   - `brew install you/tap/deadreckon`
   - `cargo binstall deadreckon` (free)
2. **For the npm/bun channel, decide:**
   - *Quick path*: ship dist's built-in npm installer. UX is `bun install -g deadreckon` → wrapper postinstalls a binary from GitHub Releases. Works for 95% of users.
   - *Claude-Code-grade path*: also publish via `cargo-npm` (or a small CI script that splits dist's archives into platform packages) so you get the optionalDependencies pattern. This is what survives `--ignore-scripts`, corporate proxies, and matches what Anthropic ships.
3. **Self-update**: embed `axoupdater` as a crate and wire `deadreckon update` as a clap subcommand. End user runs `deadreckon update`. For users on the npm/bun channel, document `bun update -g deadreckon` as the alternative — and have `deadreckon update` detect the install source and print the right hint rather than swapping a binary it doesn't own.
4. **macOS**: codesign + notarize in the dist-generated GitHub Actions workflow. Budget half a day to set up `APPLE_ID`, `TEAM_ID`, app-specific password, and the Developer ID cert as repo secrets.
5. **Linux glibc**: build with `cargo-zigbuild` (dist supports it) targeting glibc 2.17/2.28 so you don't get bug reports from Debian stable users.

End-user UX, by channel:

```
# macOS / Linux one-liner
curl -LsSf https://github.com/you/deadreckon/releases/latest/download/deadreckon-installer.sh | sh

# bun / npm / pnpm
bun install -g deadreckon
npx deadreckon          # or: bunx deadreckon

# Homebrew
brew install you/tap/deadreckon

# Rust users
cargo binstall deadreckon

# Update (any channel)
deadreckon update
```

# Distribution research summary

**The recommended stack:**

1. **Build/release**: [`dist`](https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist) (formerly `cargo-dist`) — one command (`dist init` + git tag) generates a GitHub Actions workflow that fans out across darwin-arm64/x64, linux-x64/arm64, win32-x64, produces archives + a shell installer + Homebrew tap + npm package.
2. **bun/npm channel**: dist's built-in npm installer publishes a single wrapper that postinstall-downloads from GitHub Releases. End-user UX is exactly what you asked for: `bun install -g deadreckon` or `bunx deadreckon`.
   - **Important nuance**: this is *not* the same pattern Claude Code uses. Claude Code (and esbuild, biome, swc) use `optionalDependencies` with per-platform packages (`deadreckon-darwin-arm64`, etc.) and `os`/`cpu` filters — no postinstall download. That pattern survives `--ignore-scripts`, corporate proxies, and offline caches. If you want Claude-Code-grade robustness on the npm channel, add [`cargo-npm`](https://github.com/abemedia/cargo-npm) alongside dist.
3. **Self-update**: embed [`axoupdater`](https://github.com/axodotdev/axoupdater) as a crate → wire `deadreckon update` as a clap subcommand. It re-runs the installer against the latest GitHub release.
4. **macOS Gatekeeper tax**: budget half a day for Apple Developer ID + `codesign` + `notarytool` in the dist-generated workflow, or users will see "developer cannot be verified."
5. **Linux glibc**: use `cargo-zigbuild` (dist supports it) pinned to glibc 2.17/2.28 so Debian-stable users don't file bugs.

**End-user UX you'd ship:**
```
curl -LsSf https://.../deadreckon-installer.sh | sh   # macOS/Linux one-liner
bun install -g deadreckon                              # bun/npm/pnpm
brew install you/tap/deadreckon                        # Homebrew
cargo binstall deadreckon                              # Rust users (free w/ dist)
deadreckon update                                      # self-update, any channel
```

**Bun-specific finding**: bun is npm-registry-compatible, honors `optionalDependencies` + `os`/`cpu`, and adds `--cpu`/`--os` flags for forcing cross-target installs in Docker. No bun-specific bundling step is needed — `bun build --compile` is for JS, not for shipping a Rust binary. The npm pattern works identically under bun.

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-12 02:41:19Z)**_

Honest answer: there isn't one — Windows PowerShell can't run `curl | sh`, so every "universal" installer is really two side-by-side commands or assumes a runtime. The two realistic options:

**Option A — assume a node-family runtime, get true cross-platform with one command:**
```
bun install -g deadreckon       # or: npm i -g / pnpm add -g
```
Works identically on macOS, Linux, and Windows. This is what Claude Code chose, and the reason: it's the only "one command, every OS" answer that exists today. Cost: users without bun/node have to install one first.

**Option B — zero runtime dependency, but two commands:**
```
# macOS / Linux
curl -LsSf https://github.com/you/deadreckon/releases/latest/download/deadreckon-installer.sh | sh

# Windows
irm https://github.com/you/deadreckon/releases/latest/download/deadreckon-installer.ps1 | iex
```
Both are generated for free by `dist init`. This is what rustup, deno, and bun itself ship — they document the pair side-by-side and call it "the install command." Users perceive it as one command because they only run the one for their OS.

**Recommendation:** ship both. Lead with `bun install -g deadreckon` in your README (closest to "single command works everywhere"), then list the curl/irm pair underneath for users who don't want a node runtime. `dist` produces both with no extra work, and they all resolve to the same GitHub Release artifacts, so `deadreckon update` works regardless of which one the user used.

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-12 02:42:46Z)**_

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-7 2026-05-12 02:42:53Z)**_

Short answer: **not automatically, unless you build the check into the binary itself.**

What each piece gives you:

- **`bun install -g deadreckon`** — does not auto-update. User has to run `bun update -g deadreckon`. Same for npm/pnpm/brew/cargo. Package managers don't poll.
- **`dist`'s shell/powershell installer** — installs once, never checks again.
- **`axoupdater` (or `self_update`) embedded in your binary** — gives you the `deadreckon update` *command*, but the user still has to run it.

**To make it actually auto-update**, you wire a check into `deadreckon`'s startup path:

1. On launch, async-check GitHub Releases for a newer tag (cache the result for ~24h in `~/.deadreckon/update-check.json` so you don't hammer the API).
2. If a new version exists, either:
   - **Prompt mode** — print `→ v0.2.0 available. Run \`deadreckon update\`.` and continue. Safer, predictable.
   - **Auto mode** — call axoupdater in the background, swap the binary, tell the user on next launch. This is what Claude Code does, and it detects the install channel: if you came in via npm it runs `npm update`; if via the native installer it does a binary swap.

The whole thing is ~50 lines using `axoupdater` as a library + a `tokio::spawn` on startup. The detect-install-channel logic is the only fiddly part — axoupdater exposes `InstallReceipt` for this (dist drops a receipt file at install time recording how the user installed).

So: yes, achievable; ships as part of your binary, not as part of the install command; works the same regardless of whether the user used `bun install -g` or the curl-pipe-sh installer.

# Goal & Rider Author

A two-document pattern for briefing an autonomous coding agent
(Claude Code, Codex CLI, or any agentic harness) on the next round of
work. The **goal**
is the ≤4000-char spine: what to do, what to read first, the posture,
the verification, the stop conditions. The **rider** holds the
prescriptive detail: data schemas, phase plans, depth-test names,
verb signatures, error footers, out-of-scope lists.

The pattern's superpower is that the goal stays small enough to paste
into a Codex `/goal` or a Claude run prompt, while the rider can be
arbitrarily detailed without bloating the executor's working memory.

This skill is project-agnostic. It works for any codebase that has a
`docs/goals/` (or equivalent) directory, conventional commits, and
some form of AS-BUILT / architecture doc. Substitute the project's
own toolchain commands wherever the templates say
`<project's ... command>`.

## When to invoke

The user is about to start a new round of agentic work and wants
goal+rider files written into a project's `docs/goals/` directory.
Triggers include "draft a goal that addresses X", "write a goal+rider
for Y", "new goal for the next agentic turn", "rider for X".

## Pre-work — do not skip

Before drafting, gather context. Read in this order, skipping items
the project doesn't have:

1. **Project architecture doc** — `AS-BUILT-ARCHITECTURE.md`,
   `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `docs/architecture.md`, or whatever the project
   uses. Look for a "what's shipped vs thin" section if one exists;
   it grounds the goal in reality.
2. **Prior goal+rider pairs** in `docs/goals/` (or wherever the
   project keeps them). Their invariants compose forward; do not
   duplicate verbatim. Skim the most recent two pairs to absorb
   voice and section conventions.
3. **Recent commits**: `git log --oneline -30 -- docs/goals/` and
   `git log --oneline -30`. Reveals delivery cadence and the
   conventional-commit format the project uses.
4. **Source code at HEAD** for any data structures, file paths, or
   function names you'll quote in the rider. Verify they match HEAD
   before citing.
5. **Research or pain-point reports** the project has (e.g.,
   unmet-needs, user-research, retro docs). They ground the
   ergonomics in real pain.

If you can't find prior pairs or an architecture doc, **ask the user**
for a pointer — don't invent one.

## Goal document recipe (≤4000 chars)

**Path:** `<project>/docs/goals/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<HHMM>-<project-slug>-<topic>-goal.md`

The `<HHMM>` is the local 24-hour clock time when the file is created
(e.g., `1444` for 2:44 PM). It makes `ls docs/goals/` sort in true
authoring order rather than alphabetical by topic. When two pairs land
within the same minute, secondary alphabetical sort handles the tiebreak;
that's fine.

**Hard cap:** `wc -c <file>` must be ≤4000 (prior precedents: 3929–4112).
Re-check after every edit pass. Note the `-HHMM-` insert costs ~5 chars
per internal rider reference, so leave a small buffer when riders cross-cite.

**Skeleton** — fill each section, cut to fit:

```markdown
GOAL: <one-sentence headline>. <one paragraph: current pain → what the goal lands → headline word (Friendliness / Multi-agent / Self-documenting / Default mode / …)>.

**Read first.**

- `<absolute path to project architecture doc>` — substrate; one line.
- `<absolute path to the rider being written>` — schemas, signatures, depth tests.
- `<absolute paths to exemplars or research reports>` — grounding.
- Prior riders in `<absolute path to docs/goals/>` — invariants hold.

**Posture.** Stays `<tier>`. No `<struct>` schema changes (if applicable). No `git push`. Edits inside `<project root>`. Major architectural decisions → `<V1-CANDIDATES path>`.

<DOMAIN BODY — one or two of these, depending on the goal:>

**<N> modes / verbs / artifacts, auto-resolved.**

- **`<name>`** — <one line of behavior>.

**New verbs.**

- `<verb> <args>` — <one line>.

**Friendliness as a verifiable contract.**

- Auto-detect, don't ask (the obvious case is the default).
- Preflight + preview before any state change.
- Refuse with `try: <command>` lines.
- Rollback is one command.
- Lifecycle hints after every action.

**Phases.** Eleven (P1–P11) in the rider. Each: depth test first → implement → `<project's build+test+lint+fmt command>` green → conventional-commit → CHANGELOG. P11 adds a `<new section>` to the project architecture doc.

**Verification.**

- Commands green every commit; every rider depth test present and passing.
- <Smoke 1>: <verifiable command + assertion>.
- <Smoke 2>: <verifiable command + assertion>.
- No edits outside `<project>`. No `git push`. No schema changes.

**Stop when** verification passes, AS-BUILT updated, CHANGELOG has a "<Milestone name> (alpha)" section, committed locally.
```

**Trim priority when over budget:**

1. Drop parenthetical detail that's already in the rider.
2. Shorten Read-first descriptions to bare absolute paths.
3. Compress Posture to one or two lines.
4. Cut verification smoke bullets to two.
5. Drop cross-rider "do not preempt" notes; those live in the rider.

## Rider document recipe (no char cap; typically 10–35K)

**Path:** `<project>/docs/goals/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<HHMM>-<project-slug>-<topic>-rider.md`

Use the **same** `<YYYY-MM-DD>-<HHMM>` prefix as the matching goal so
the pair sorts together. Author the goal first, then mirror its
timestamp on the rider — never split them across minutes.

**Skeleton:**

```markdown
# <project> — <Slug> Rider (<short framing>)

This rider holds the prescriptive constraints for the goal at
`<absolute path to goal>`. It supersedes nothing in prior riders
(<list dated rider filenames>) — their invariants still apply.
This rider adds <one-line summary of what's new>.

**All paths absolute.** Source `<project root>`, runtime `<runtime root>`.

## Posture (decided — do not redesign)

- **Maturity stays `<tier>`** (alpha / beta / stable; mirrors what
  the project calls the current milestone).
- **No `<struct>` schema changes** (if applicable). State lives in

- **Edits stay inside `<project root>`.**

## Data model (files, not fields)

<JSON schemas for any new file-based state. One block per file.
Inline-comment each field if the meaning isn't obvious.>

## <Algorithms / Mode resolution / Detection rules>

<Pseudocode for non-obvious logic. The rider IS the spec — match it
in the implementation.>

## Verb signatures

```
<verb> <args>
    [--flag]                  # description
    [--other-flag <type>]     # description
```

For each verb: refusal cases table.

## Phases (eleven)

Each phase: write the named depth test(s) **first** and watch them
fail; implement; green on
`<project's build+test+lint+fmt command, green on each commit>`;
conventional-commit local commit; one-line CHANGELOG entry.

### P1 — <name>

- `snake_case_descriptive_name_that_would_have_caught_the_thin_behavior`

### P2 — <name>

...

### P11 — Architecture doc update + CHANGELOG (doc only; no depth test)

- Insert a new top-level section into `<architecture doc path>`:
  ```
  ## NN. <Section title>

  NN.1 <subsection>
  NN.2 <subsection>
  ...
  ```
- If the architecture doc has a "what's shipped vs thin" section,
  update it:
  - Add to the "shipped" side: <items this rider lands>.
  - Note explicitly whether this rider closes prior thin items or
    only adds capability.
- Append to `<CHANGELOG path>`:
  ```

  ```

## Integration matrix (when multi-mode or multi-verb)

| <axis> | <feature 1> | <feature 2> | … |
|---|---|---|---|
| ... | ... | ... | ... |

## Error-footer canonical pairs

| Error | `try:` |
|---|---|
| `<terse description>` | `<one specific command or fix>` |

(Parameterized over a depth test so every error case is exercised.)

## Config additions (when relevant)

```toml
[defaults]
<new_knob> = "<default>"
```

## Out of scope (explicitly not in this milestone)

- <one bullet per V1-candidate scope item>
- <…>

## Dependencies (Tier 1 / 2 / 3 policy)

Tier 1 (utility, free): <list with one-line justification each>.
Tier 2 (architectural, log to `DEPENDENCIES.md`): <list or "none expected">.
Tier 3 (blocked): same blocks as prior riders.

## Engineering invariants (do not violate)

- **No `<struct>` schema changes.**
- **One depth test before each phase implementation.** A phase whose
  tests were never red is suspect.
- **<Domain-specific invariants>.**
- **No silent expansion.** Anything beyond P1–P11 goes into
  `V1-CANDIDATES.md`.
- **<Spec-pinning invariants>**: e.g., "the preview block format is
  depth-tested; changing whitespace changes the spec."

## Process invariants

- Phased local commits only. No `git push`.
- Each phase ends with the relevant depth tests passing and a
  CHANGELOG entry naming the SHA.
- After P11, optionally capture a demo (asciinema cast / screenshots /
  short video) under `<project>/<demo-path>`. Skip when the change
  isn't user-visible.
- If a phase reveals a V1-architecture decision, stop and log it in
  `V1-CANDIDATES.md`; do not silently expand scope.
```

## Discipline checklist (the invariants this skill carries)

1. **Two documents, two budgets.** Goal ≤4000 chars; rider unbounded.
   Run `wc -c` on the goal before declaring done.
2. **Timestamped filenames.** Both goal and rider are named
   `<YYYY-MM-DD>-<HHMM>-<project-slug>-<topic>-{goal,rider}.md`. The
   `<HHMM>` is the local 24-hour authoring time (e.g., `1444`). The
   pair shares one timestamp so they sort together; never split them
   across minutes. This makes `ls docs/goals/` chronological.
3. **Phased local commits only.** Never tell the executor to `git push`.
4. **Files-not-fields.** When the project has persistent state
   structs (DB schema, config struct, state machine), durable
   per-feature state should live in files inside the working tree
   (`<some>/<name>.json`) rather than as new struct fields. Schema
   changes are last-resort. Skip this invariant for projects without
   such structs.
5. **Depth tests first.** Each phase's named tests are written and
   watched fail before implementation. List them by name in the rider
   so a `grep -c '^    fn '` enforces presence.
6. **Architecture-doc discipline.** P11 always updates whatever
   architecture / as-built doc the project keeps, plus CHANGELOG. If
   there's a "what's shipped vs thin" section, the thin list is
   honest — only remove items the rider actually closes.
7. **V1 candidates.** Anything out of scope goes to
   `docs/V1-CANDIDATES.md`, not silently expanded scope.
8. **Conventional commits, scoped.** `docs(goals): add <topic> goal+rider`
   for the goal-rider commit itself. `feat(<scope>):` / `fix(<scope>):`
   / `chore(<scope>):` for execution commits.
9. **Frontmatter mirrors the project's own convention** for any
   human-readable artifacts. If the project has prior impl docs
   under `docs/implementation/` or similar, match their frontmatter
   shape (Date / Status / Commit span / Owner / …). If not, propose
   a minimal frontmatter and stick to it across riders.
10. **Friendliness is verifiable.** Auto-detect, preflight + preview,
    refuse with `try: <command>`, one-command rollback, lifecycle
    hints. Each is exercised by a depth test.
11. **Judgment in markdown, invariants in code.** When the project
    has a skill / prompt-template / config-driven prompt mechanism,
    prefer that over a hardcoded const so users can tune voice or
    behavior without a rebuild. (Project-specific; skip if no such
    mechanism exists.)

## Anti-patterns to avoid

- Inventing V1 architecture inside an alpha rider.
- Schema changes without a stated strong reason.
- Backwards-compatibility shims for code that no caller uses.
- Comments explaining WHAT the code does (well-named identifiers
  already do that).
- Half-finished implementations ("we'll finish in P12").
- Duplicating invariants from prior riders verbatim — just say
  "invariants hold" and reference them.
- Depth tests written after implementation.
- Stop conditions that don't tie to verification ("stop when it
  feels done" is not a stop condition).
- Inventing CLI verbs not in the goal.
- Adding emojis to written artifacts.
- "TODO: maybe add X" lines — either it's in scope (P-numbered) or
  it's a V1 candidate.

## Standard 11-phase shape

A typical rider has these phases (adapt the names; eleven is a target,
not a hard rule — fewer or more is fine if the structure earns it):

- **P1**: Data model / plumbing — new module / file path / frontmatter
  helpers. No behavior change yet.
- **P2–P3**: Foundation — new primitive types, base mechanism.
- **P4–P8**: Feature implementation — one phase per major slice; each
  phase ships with end-to-end depth tests.
- **P9**: Integration with prior verbs / modes / state machines.
- **P10**: Cross-cutting friendliness pass — flags like `--quiet` /
  `--plain`, error-footer routing, post-action hints, help-text
  grouping.
- **P11**: Architecture-doc update + CHANGELOG + (optional) demo
  capture (doc-only; no depth test).

## Commit message for the goal-rider pair itself

```
docs(goals): add <topic> goal+rider (<one-line headline>)

<2–3 sentence summary: what the goal is for; what the rider prescribes;
what's explicitly out of scope. Mention named depth-test discipline,
files-not-fields posture (if applicable), V1 invention guard.>
```

Add the project's standard `Co-Authored-By:` footer if it uses one.

RIDER=$PROJECT/docs/goals/$DATE-$HHMM-$PROJECT_SLUG-$TOPIC-rider.md

# 2. Rider must have ≥11 phase headers

# Goal & Rider Author

A two-document pattern for briefing an autonomous coding agent
(Claude Code, Codex CLI, or any agentic harness) on the next round of
work. The **goal**
is the ≤4000-char spine: what to do, what to read first, the posture,
the verification, the stop conditions. The **rider** holds the
prescriptive detail: data schemas, phase plans, depth-test names,
verb signatures, error footers, out-of-scope lists.

The pattern's superpower is that the goal stays small enough to paste
into a Codex `/goal` or a Claude run prompt, while the rider can be
arbitrarily detailed without bloating the executor's working memory.

This skill is project-agnostic. It works for any codebase that has a
`docs/goals/` (or equivalent) directory, conventional commits, and
some form of AS-BUILT / architecture doc. Substitute the project's
own toolchain commands wherever the templates say
`<project's ... command>`.

## When to invoke

The user is about to start a new round of agentic work and wants
goal+rider files written into a project's `docs/goals/` directory.
Triggers include "draft a goal that addresses X", "write a goal+rider
for Y", "new goal for the next agentic turn", "rider for X".

## Pre-work — do not skip

Before drafting, gather context. Read in this order, skipping items
the project doesn't have:

1. **Project architecture doc** — `AS-BUILT-ARCHITECTURE.md`,
   `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `docs/architecture.md`, or whatever the project
   uses. Look for a "what's shipped vs thin" section if one exists;
   it grounds the goal in reality.
2. **Prior goal+rider pairs** in `docs/goals/` (or wherever the
   project keeps them). Their invariants compose forward; do not
   duplicate verbatim. Skim the most recent two pairs to absorb
   voice and section conventions.
3. **Recent commits**: `git log --oneline -30 -- docs/goals/` and
   `git log --oneline -30`. Reveals delivery cadence and the
   conventional-commit format the project uses.
4. **Source code at HEAD** for any data structures, file paths, or
   function names you'll quote in the rider. Verify they match HEAD
   before citing.
5. **Research or pain-point reports** the project has (e.g.,
   unmet-needs, user-research, retro docs). They ground the
   ergonomics in real pain.

If you can't find prior pairs or an architecture doc, **ask the user**
for a pointer — don't invent one.

## Goal document recipe (≤4000 chars)

**Path:** `<project>/docs/goals/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<HHMM>-<project-slug>-<topic>-goal.md`

The `<HHMM>` is the local 24-hour clock time when the file is created
(e.g., `1444` for 2:44 PM). It makes `ls docs/goals/` sort in true
authoring order rather than alphabetical by topic. When two pairs land
within the same minute, secondary alphabetical sort handles the tiebreak;
that's fine.

**Hard cap:** `wc -c <file>` must be ≤4000 (prior precedents: 3929–4112).
Re-check after every edit pass. Note the `-HHMM-` insert costs ~5 chars
per internal rider reference, so leave a small buffer when riders cross-cite.

**Skeleton** — fill each section, cut to fit:

```markdown
GOAL: <one-sentence headline>. <one paragraph: current pain → what the goal lands → headline word (Friendliness / Multi-agent / Self-documenting / Default mode / …)>.

**Read first.**

- `<absolute path to project architecture doc>` — substrate; one line.
- `<absolute path to the rider being written>` — schemas, signatures, depth tests.
- `<absolute paths to exemplars or research reports>` — grounding.
- Prior riders in `<absolute path to docs/goals/>` — invariants hold.

**Posture.** Stays `<tier>`. No `<struct>` schema changes (if applicable). No `git push`. Edits inside `<project root>`. Major architectural decisions → `<V1-CANDIDATES path>`.

<DOMAIN BODY — one or two of these, depending on the goal:>

**<N> modes / verbs / artifacts, auto-resolved.**

- **`<name>`** — <one line of behavior>.

**New verbs.**

- `<verb> <args>` — <one line>.

**Friendliness as a verifiable contract.**

- Auto-detect, don't ask (the obvious case is the default).
- Preflight + preview before any state change.
- Refuse with `try: <command>` lines.
- Rollback is one command.
- Lifecycle hints after every action.

**Phases.** Eleven (P1–P11) in the rider. Each: depth test first → implement → `<project's build+test+lint+fmt command>` green → conventional-commit → CHANGELOG. P11 adds a `<new section>` to the project architecture doc.

**Verification.**

- Commands green every commit; every rider depth test present and passing.
- <Smoke 1>: <verifiable command + assertion>.
- <Smoke 2>: <verifiable command + assertion>.
- No edits outside `<project>`. No `git push`. No schema changes.

**Stop when** verification passes, AS-BUILT updated, CHANGELOG has a "<Milestone name> (alpha)" section, committed locally.
```

**Trim priority when over budget:**

1. Drop parenthetical detail that's already in the rider.
2. Shorten Read-first descriptions to bare absolute paths.
3. Compress Posture to one or two lines.
4. Cut verification smoke bullets to two.
5. Drop cross-rider "do not preempt" notes; those live in the rider.

## Rider document recipe (no char cap; typically 10–35K)

**Path:** `<project>/docs/goals/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<HHMM>-<project-slug>-<topic>-rider.md`

Use the **same** `<YYYY-MM-DD>-<HHMM>` prefix as the matching goal so
the pair sorts together. Author the goal first, then mirror its
timestamp on the rider — never split them across minutes.

**Skeleton:**

```markdown
# <project> — <Slug> Rider (<short framing>)

This rider holds the prescriptive constraints for the goal at
`<absolute path to goal>`. It supersedes nothing in prior riders
(<list dated rider filenames>) — their invariants still apply.
This rider adds <one-line summary of what's new>.

**All paths absolute.** Source `<project root>`, runtime `<runtime root>`.

## Posture (decided — do not redesign)

- **Maturity stays `<tier>`** (alpha / beta / stable; mirrors what
  the project calls the current milestone).
- **No `<struct>` schema changes** (if applicable). State lives in
  files at `<path>`.
- **<Other domain-specific invariants — be explicit>.**
- **No `git push`.** Phased local commits only.
- **No V1 / next-tier invention.** If a phase reveals a major
  architectural decision, log it in `<V1-CANDIDATES path>` (or
  equivalent) and continue.
- **Edits stay inside `<project root>`.**

## Data model (files, not fields)

<JSON schemas for any new file-based state. One block per file.
Inline-comment each field if the meaning isn't obvious.>

## <Algorithms / Mode resolution / Detection rules>

<Pseudocode for non-obvious logic. The rider IS the spec — match it
in the implementation.>

## Verb signatures

```
<verb> <args>
    [--flag]                  # description
    [--other-flag <type>]     # description
```

For each verb: refusal cases table.

## Phases (eleven)

Each phase: write the named depth test(s) **first** and watch them
fail; implement; green on
`<project's build+test+lint+fmt command, green on each commit>`;
conventional-commit local commit; one-line CHANGELOG entry.

### P1 — <name>

- <bulleted prescriptions>

Depth tests (in `<test path>`):
- `snake_case_descriptive_name_that_would_have_caught_the_thin_behavior`
- `another_named_test`

### P2 — <name>

...

### P11 — Architecture doc update + CHANGELOG (doc only; no depth test)

- Insert a new top-level section into `<architecture doc path>`:
  ```
  ## NN. <Section title>

  NN.1 <subsection>
  NN.2 <subsection>
  ...
  ```
- If the architecture doc has a "what's shipped vs thin" section,
  update it:
  - Add to the "shipped" side: <items this rider lands>.
  - Note explicitly whether this rider closes prior thin items or
    only adds capability.
- Append to `<CHANGELOG path>`:
  ```
  ## <Milestone name> (<tier>) — <YYYY-MM-DD>

  - <bullet>
  ```

## Integration matrix (when multi-mode or multi-verb)

| <axis> | <feature 1> | <feature 2> | … |
|---|---|---|---|
| ... | ... | ... | ... |

## Error-footer canonical pairs

| Error | `try:` |
|---|---|
| `<terse description>` | `<one specific command or fix>` |

(Parameterized over a depth test so every error case is exercised.)

## Config additions (when relevant)

```toml
[defaults]
<new_knob> = "<default>"
```

## Out of scope (explicitly not in this milestone)

- <one bullet per V1-candidate scope item>
- <…>

## Dependencies (Tier 1 / 2 / 3 policy)

Tier 1 (utility, free): <list with one-line justification each>.
Tier 2 (architectural, log to `DEPENDENCIES.md`): <list or "none expected">.
Tier 3 (blocked): same blocks as prior riders.

## Engineering invariants (do not violate)

- **No `<struct>` schema changes.**
- **One depth test before each phase implementation.** A phase whose
  tests were never red is suspect.
- **<Domain-specific invariants>.**
- **No silent expansion.** Anything beyond P1–P11 goes into
  `V1-CANDIDATES.md`.
- **<Spec-pinning invariants>**: e.g., "the preview block format is
  depth-tested; changing whitespace changes the spec."

## Process invariants

- Phased local commits only. No `git push`.
- Each phase ends with the relevant depth tests passing and a
  CHANGELOG entry naming the SHA.
- After P11, optionally capture a demo (asciinema cast / screenshots /
  short video) under `<project>/<demo-path>`. Skip when the change
  isn't user-visible.
- If a phase reveals a V1-architecture decision, stop and log it in
  `V1-CANDIDATES.md`; do not silently expand scope.
```

## Discipline checklist (the invariants this skill carries)

1. **Two documents, two budgets.** Goal ≤4000 chars; rider unbounded.
   Run `wc -c` on the goal before declaring done.
2. **Timestamped filenames.** Both goal and rider are named
   `<YYYY-MM-DD>-<HHMM>-<project-slug>-<topic>-{goal,rider}.md`. The
   `<HHMM>` is the local 24-hour authoring time (e.g., `1444`). The
   pair shares one timestamp so they sort together; never split them
   across minutes. This makes `ls docs/goals/` chronological.
3. **Phased local commits only.** Never tell the executor to `git push`.
4. **Files-not-fields.** When the project has persistent state
   structs (DB schema, config struct, state machine), durable
   per-feature state should live in files inside the working tree
   (`<some>/<name>.json`) rather than as new struct fields. Schema
   changes are last-resort. Skip this invariant for projects without
   such structs.
5. **Depth tests first.** Each phase's named tests are written and
   watched fail before implementation. List them by name in the rider
   so a `grep -c '^    fn '` enforces presence.
6. **Architecture-doc discipline.** P11 always updates whatever
   architecture / as-built doc the project keeps, plus CHANGELOG. If
   there's a "what's shipped vs thin" section, the thin list is
   honest — only remove items the rider actually closes.
7. **V1 candidates.** Anything out of scope goes to
   `docs/V1-CANDIDATES.md`, not silently expanded scope.
8. **Conventional commits, scoped.** `docs(goals): add <topic> goal+rider`
   for the goal-rider commit itself. `feat(<scope>):` / `fix(<scope>):`
   / `chore(<scope>):` for execution commits.
9. **Frontmatter mirrors the project's own convention** for any
   human-readable artifacts. If the project has prior impl docs
   under `docs/implementation/` or similar, match their frontmatter
   shape (Date / Status / Commit span / Owner / …). If not, propose
   a minimal frontmatter and stick to it across riders.
10. **Friendliness is verifiable.** Auto-detect, preflight + preview,
    refuse with `try: <command>`, one-command rollback, lifecycle
    hints. Each is exercised by a depth test.
11. **Judgment in markdown, invariants in code.** When the project
    has a skill / prompt-template / config-driven prompt mechanism,
    prefer that over a hardcoded const so users can tune voice or
    behavior without a rebuild. (Project-specific; skip if no such
    mechanism exists.)

## Anti-patterns to avoid

- Inventing V1 architecture inside an alpha rider.
- Schema changes without a stated strong reason.
- Backwards-compatibility shims for code that no caller uses.
- Comments explaining WHAT the code does (well-named identifiers
  already do that).
- Half-finished implementations ("we'll finish in P12").
- Duplicating invariants from prior riders verbatim — just say
  "invariants hold" and reference them.
- Depth tests written after implementation.
- Stop conditions that don't tie to verification ("stop when it
  feels done" is not a stop condition).
- Inventing CLI verbs not in the goal.
- Adding emojis to written artifacts.
- "TODO: maybe add X" lines — either it's in scope (P-numbered) or
  it's a V1 candidate.

A typical rider has these phases (adapt the names; eleven is a target,
not a hard rule — fewer or more is fine if the structure earns it):

- **P1**: Data model / plumbing — new module / file path / frontmatter

- **P9**: Integration with prior verbs / modes / state machines.
- **P10**: Cross-cutting friendliness pass — flags like `--quiet` /
  `--plain`, error-footer routing, post-action hints, help-text
  grouping.
- **P11**: Architecture-doc update + CHANGELOG + (optional) demo
  capture (doc-only; no depth test).

1	GOAL: Polish deadreckon at `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/` for true overnight operation. Today an unattended `run` survives flakes but the surrounding UX is bare — no caffeinate (laptop sleeps mid-turn), a plain-text preview, a silent "completed" line, and globally-signed per-turn commits can hang on pinentry. This goal lands a card-shaped CLI vocabulary (preview / exit / status / show / list), `--prevent-sleep` on macOS + Linux, and unattended-git hardening so a run started before bed is still a run in the morning. Headline word: **Overnight**.
2	
3	**Read first.**
4	
5	- `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/AS-BUILT-ARCHITECTURE.md` — substrate; especially §17 CLI, §18 TUI, §22 thin.
6	- `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/goals/2026-05-11-2248-deadreckon-overnight-rider.md` — card primitives, schemas, depth tests, sleep-handshake shape, phase plan.
7	- gnhf exemplars: `https://github.com/kunchenguid/gnhf` (`src/core/{exit-summary,sleep,git}.ts`) — aesthetic + systemd-inhibit handshake to mine.
8	- Prior riders in `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/goals/` — invariants hold; doctor + status polish lightly overlap audit-harden P7/P10 (rider says how to land non-conflicting).
9	
10	**Posture.** Stays `alpha`. No `PipelineState` schema changes — sleep state in `working/.deadreckon/sleep-prevention.json`. No `git push`. Edits inside `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/`. Major decisions → `docs/V1-CANDIDATES.md`.
11	
12	**Two pillars: caffeinate + cards.**
13	
14	- **`--prevent-sleep <auto|on|off>`.** Defaults on under TTY, off under non-TTY, config-overridable. macOS spawns `caffeinate -di` for the run lifetime; Linux re-execs under `systemd-inhibit` with a tmpfs ready-path handshake (trusted-path checked both sides); Windows `doctor` reports unsupported. `sleep-prevention.json` records mode+pid; reap on every exit path.
15	- **One card renderer for every user-facing surface.** `ui_card` primitive — ANSI-safe length, terminal-width capped, `--plain` strips color and box-drawing, golden-file pinned. Pre-run **preview card** (mode/branch/base/worktree/provider+model/caps/sleep); end-of-run **exit summary card** (turns, spend with `~` when any turn subscription/estimated, files added/updated/deleted, snapshots, gate status, attach+show+apply hints). `status`, `show`, `list`, and the attach completion footer converge onto the same primitives.
16	
17	**Unattended-git hardening.** Every `git` invocation in `deadreckon-core` and `deadreckon` routes through one helper that exports `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` and inserts `-c commit.gpgsign=false -c tag.gpgsign=false` on commit-family verbs. No pinentry hangs on globally-signed checkouts. A depth test greps for raw `Command::new("git")` outside the helper.
18	
19	**Friendliness.** Auto-detect TTY for default sleep prevention; preview before any state change; refuse with `try: <command>` on every footer; rollback is one command (`undo`/`discard`). `--plain` + `NO_COLOR` strip to ASCII; <40-col terminals fall back without crashing.
20	
21	**Phases.** Eleven (P1–P11) in the rider. Each: depth test first → implement → `cargo build --release && cargo test --workspace && cargo clippy --workspace -- -D warnings && cargo fmt --check` green → conventional-commit → CHANGELOG. P11 adds §26 "Overnight UX" to AS-BUILT, updates §22.

41	
42	## 1. System Overview & Mental Model
43	
44	deadreckon is a Rust 2024 CLI harness whose default flow is **unattended long-running coding tasks**: `deadreckon run <goal>` creates durable run state, picks a BYOK provider route, executes turns inside a platform-native sandbox, writes spend/provenance/trace records after every turn, and exits only when the LLM declares done, a budget caps the run, or the operator kills it. The CLI is the user-facing layer; the `deadreckon-core` library owns the deterministic primitives (state, locks, gates, snapshots, atomic file ops); `deadreckon-providers` and `deadreckon-sandbox` are pluggable layers underneath.
45	
46	```
47	┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
48	│ USER                                                                      │
49	│ deadreckon run "make a hello-world Rust binary" --max-spend 5             │
50	└────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┘
51	                                 │
52	┌────────────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────────────┐
53	│ CLI LAYER (crates/deadreckon)                                             │
54	│   main.rs:316  run_command()                                              │
55	│   main.rs:940  resume_command()  ← refuses Completed at :947              │
56	│   main.rs:874  attach_command()  ← ratatui TUI                            │
57	│   main.rs:484  doctor_command()                                           │
58	│   main.rs:241  init_command()                                             │
59	│ ◆ clap parsing  ◆ ratatui rendering  ◆ post-run summary                   │
60	└────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┘
61	                                 │ create_run → acquire_lock → run_turn_loop
62	                                 ▼
63	┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
64	│ CORE LIBRARY (crates/deadreckon-core)                                     │
65	│                                                                           │
66	│  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐ │
67	│  │ state.rs     │  │ lock.rs      │  │ promotion.rs │  │ turn_loop.rs │ │
68	│  │ ─Pipeline    │  │ ─PID-aware   │  │ ─atomic      │  │ ─the loop    │ │
69	│  │   State      │  │  locks       │  │  working→    │  │   load-      │ │
70	│  │ ─RunStatus   │  │ ─heartbeats  │  │  library swap │  │  bearing    │ │
71	│  │ ─PhaseId     │  │ ─stale       │  │ ─manifest.json│  │ ─snapshots  │ │
72	│  │              │  │  reclaim     │  │              │  │ ─dispatch   │ │
73	│  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘ │
74	│  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐ │
75	│  │ gate.rs      │  │ artifacts.rs │  │ paths.rs     │  │ events.rs    │ │
76	│  │ ─Acceptance  │  │ ─copy_tree   │  │ ─DeadreckonPaths│ ─RunEventBus │ │
77	│  │   Marker     │  │ ─snapshot    │  │ ─scope hash  │  │ ─broadcast   │ │
78	│  │ ─signature   │  │ ─append_*    │  │ ─task_key    │  │  channel     │ │
79	│  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘ │
80	└──┬──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┬───────────┘
81	   │ ProviderRouter::complete │ run_sandbox(SandboxSpec)        │ tracing
82	   ▼                          ▼                                 ▼
83	┌─────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────┐         ┌────────────────┐
84	│ PROVIDERS       │   │ SANDBOX              │         │ RUNTIME STATE  │
85	│ HTTP:           │   │ sandbox-exec (mac)   │         │ ~/.deadreckon/ │
86	│  anthropic      │   │ bwrap (linux)        │         │  runstate/...  │
87	│  openai         │   │ docker (opt-in)      │         │  library/...   │
88	│  openai-compat  │   │ none (passthrough)   │         │  locks/...     │
89	│ CLI:            │   │ auto (resolves)      │         │  config.toml   │
90	│  cli:claude-code│   │ ─SIGTERM 2s → SIGKILL│         └────────────────┘
91	│  cli:codex      │   │ ─PID persisted       │
92	│ TEST:           │   │ ─cancellation token  │
93	│  smoke (scripted)│  └──────────────────────┘
94	└─────────────────┘
95	```
96	
97	Why this shape works:
98	
99	- **The CLI is thin.** It parses args, sets up state, hands off to the turn loop. All durability lives in `deadreckon-core`.
100	- **State is on disk before every meaningful change.** `state.json` is atomic-written via temp+rename after every phase transition, snapshot, spend record, and tool call.
```

2	
3	This rider holds the prescriptive constraints for the goal at

8	usability}) — their invariants still apply. This rider adds the card
9	vocabulary, caffeinate / systemd-inhibit sleep prevention, and the
10	unattended-git hardening pair that makes a pre-bedtime `run` reliably
11	outlive a closed laptop.

34	  conventional-commit per-turn preset, permanent-error stderr
35	  classification, and host SKILL.md all stay out of scope; if a phase

39	### Overlap with peer riders — land non-conflicting
40	
41	- **Audit-harden P7 (`doctor` exhaustive)** adds opt-in provider-ping
42	  rows. This rider adds two sleep-prevention rows to `doctor`. Both
43	  appear under the existing "Runtime checks" section; do not rename

57	## Data model (files, not fields)
58	
59	### `working/.deadreckon/sleep-prevention.json`
60	
61	Written when sleep prevention arms; deleted when it disarms. On crash
62	recovery, deadreckon reaps the recorded pid if alive and removes the
63	file regardless.
64	
65	```json
66	{
67	  "mode": "caffeinate",
68	  "pid": 51234,
69	  "armed_at": "2026-05-11T22:15:32Z",
70	  "inhibitor_binary": "/usr/bin/caffeinate",
71	  "reason": "deadreckon overnight run",
72	  "skip_reason": null
73	}
74	```
75	
76	Field reference:
77	
78	- `mode` — one of `"caffeinate"`, `"systemd-inhibit"`, `"none"`,
79	  `"unsupported"`.
80	- `pid` — pid of the inhibitor child (`caffeinate`) or the re-exec'd
81	  self under `systemd-inhibit`; `null` when `mode` is `"none"` or
82	  `"unsupported"`.
83	- `inhibitor_binary` — resolved path to the binary; `null` when no
84	  inhibitor was spawned.
85	- `skip_reason` — one of `"non-tty"`, `"user-disabled"`,
86	  `"unavailable"`, `"already-inhibited"`, `"unsupported"`, or `null`
87	  when armed.
88	
89	### `~/.deadreckon/config.toml` additions
90	
91	```toml
92	[defaults]
93	prevent_sleep = "auto"  # "auto" | "on" | "off"
94	plain = false           # global default for the --plain flag
95	```

5	- Added the chain data model foundation: `chain.json`, `chain-events.jsonl`, chain path helpers, chain lock task-key convention, and `RunPromoted` events after promotion.
6	
7	## Hardening v2 (alpha) — 2026-05-11
8	
9	- Added `docs/AUDIT-2026-05-11.md` mapping the original 25 unmet needs to current evidence and the P2-P10 closure plan.
10	- Replaced TUI polling-only attach with event-backed attach: same-process broadcast plus cross-process `events.jsonl` replay.
11	- Hardened cross-process cancellation with durable cancel markers, provider abort coverage, and kill-storm tests.
12	- Hardened partial-trace resume and `resume --from-turn` so trace, spend, and snapshot tails are truncated together.
13	- Added durable `sandbox.toml` per run, per-tool sandbox policy, and refusal provenance for disallowed filesystem/network actions.
14	- Expanded `acceptance.yaml` support with required/optional checks, file/content/build/shell checks, and signed per-check proof results.
15	- Made `doctor` more actionable across providers, sandboxes, OS, permissions, disk, and opt-in provider pings.
16	- Added `deadreckon library list|search|show` for promoted artifacts, including goal/date filters and promoted-doc grep.
17	- Hardened Claude Code/Codex/Cursor import normalization with source metadata, deterministic imported run IDs, stable Cursor ordering, malformed JSONL errors, and committed show-output golden tests.
18	- Polished CLI help/status/completion UX, including command groups, run health/library/disk status blocks, and `DEADRECKON_HINTS=0`.
19	- Updated `docs/AS-BUILT-ARCHITECTURE.md` and `docs/AUDIT-2026-05-11.md` with the Hardening v2 closure evidence.
20	
21	## UX consolidation — 2026-05-11
22	
23	- Added an in-TUI Markdown docs view for completed runs. Press `d` in `attach` to toggle a styled `RUN-NARRATIVE.md` rendering instead of dropping to plain terminal output.
24	- Made `deadreckon apply` idempotent when a run branch has already landed on the target branch; it now reports `already applied` and can still perform `--cleanup` instead of failing on an empty commit.
25	- Added explicit provider/model affordances: `run --model`, `extend --model`, model-aware run previews, and `deadreckon config provider|model` shortcuts.
26	- Made `deadreckon list` project-scoped by default, with `--all` for global history and `--full` for script-friendly full values.
27	- Added `latest` / `last` run-id aliases for user-facing run commands, resolved to the latest run in the current project.
28	- Added `deadreckon status` with `next` as an alias; running `deadreckon` with no subcommand now shows the current project's latest run and next action.
29	- Added `deadreckon cleanup` with `prune` as an alias for cleaned, stale, or completed worktree cleanup.
30	- Added friendlier command aliases: `export` for `materialize` and `discard` for `abandon`.
